Create offline reports from coding-agent conversations: complete messages, evidence-linked analysis, per-model token and cost comparisons, and a zoomable timeline with local day/night shading. Supports Copilot CLI, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor exports, and Replit conversation exports. Use Python 3.12 or later. Install the package and its Chromium renderer in a virtual environment: On Linux, missing browser system libraries may require python -m playwright install --with-deps chromium and system-install privileges. Report commands check rendering dependencies before processing sessions or launching an agent. The installed agent-session-insights command works from any directory. python -m agent_session_insights accepts the same arguments. For a source checkout, use python review.py after installing requirements.txt ; see the maintainer guide . If Windows activation is unavailable, invoke the virtual environment's .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe with the module or checkout entry point directly. This selects the newest matching session , freezes its logs, launches its native harness headlessly for reviewed annotations, then generates and verifies the report. The harness CLI must be on PATH and signed in; normal model charges apply. Only the selected evidence is reviewed. Use --noagent for measured accounting and replay without qualitative annotations or model calls. Automatic discovery supports Copilot, Claude, and Codex. It matches recorded repository/working-directory metadata in the current user's native history stores, not project mentions in messages, and excludes native subagents. Missing or malformed metadata limits discovery; Cursor/Replit require explicit exports . Native stores under your home are .copilot\session-state , .claude\projects , .codex\sessions , and .codex\archived_sessions . Home-directory overrides honor COPILOT_HOME , CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR , and CODEX_HOME . Repeat --session to combine selected IDs, or use --all for every match. For a combined report, the first selected session's harness reviews the evidence. --harness filters the histories searched; it does not choose a different reviewer for those histories. This writes .\collected-logs\session-logs.zip without running analysis, calling a model, or requiring Chromium/Playwright. story|title:ai privacy cloak.content_excerpt: A local proxy that sits between AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, aider, Codex CLI, ...) and the model provider's API, redacting secrets and PII before they leave your machine — and restoring them transparently in the response. Status: early scaffold / MVP in progress. Not production-ready. Name is a placeholder. Is this plug-and-play, or does it need configuration? A few one-time terminal commands, then it's invisible. There's no config file to write and cloak has no API keys or accounts of its own - cloak install detects your shell and writes one environment variable your agent already knows how to read ( ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL , or the equivalent for your provider), cloak serve (or cloak service install for something that survives reboots) starts it, and from then on you just use Claude Code / Cursor / aider exactly as before. The only ongoing interaction is cloak toggle / enable / disable if you ever want to turn redaction off without losing your agent's connection. See the full steps below. Use a real build, not go run , for anything in step 3 onward - go run compiles to a throwaway temp binary, and cloak service install needs a stable path to relaunch on login. cloak proxies one provider's API at a time: anthropic (default), openai , or gemini . This writes the right environment variable into your shell profile: Then restart your shell (or source ~/.zshrc ) so new terminal sessions pick up the variable. Pick foreground (simplest, stops when the terminal closes) or background (survives reboots): Either way, once it's running, just use Claude Code / Cursor / aider as normal - requests are redacted on the way out and restored on the way back in, with no change to your workflow. cloak-tray doesn't start or stop cloak serve - it's a thin GUI client on the same control API as step 4, so it only does anything useful while cloak is already running. macOS: unsigned by default, but package-macos.sh now signs + notarizes a real build when CLOAK_SIGN_IDENTITY and CLOAK_NOTARY_PROFILE are set (one-time Keychain setup, documented at the top of the script) - opens with no Gatekeeper warning at all once that's in place. Windows: still unsigned, no code-signing certificate owned yet - SmartScreen will warn on first run. Traditional certs run ~$200-500/yr and usually need business verification; Microsoft's newer Trusted Signing (Azure-based, pay-per-use) is worth checking as a cheaper option, but verify current pricing/eligibility directly since it's changed before.

story|title:inbox envoy an open source e.content_excerpt: Inbox Envoy: an open skill that lets your personal AI agent protect your inbox, organize mail, and research unfamiliar offers before they reach you. Public beta. Claude Code 2.1.202 running Inbox Envoy v0.1.0-beta.3 on Nov 17, 2026, sorting eight made-up emails. Nothing was connected, changed or sent. One of the eight tries to give the agent orders; it gets flagged, not obeyed. An open, portable skill that teaches an existing personal agent to protect your inbox, organize mail, highlight opportunities, and, with separate permission, investigate an uncertain unsolicited offer. When possible it researches public company documentation or published company agents (PAP, A2A, MCP); where evidence is insufficient it can prepare or, on appropriately isolated hosts, conduct a limited screening conversation. This is a skill, not an email provider, separate inbox, continuous-monitoring service, or new mailbox connector . The personal agent must already have the necessary mail tools and scheduling capability. Installation by itself never grants access or enables sending. Inbox Envoy is designed for intelligent personal agents that can load a skill (a folder with SKILL.md plus reference files) and that already have authorized access to your mailbox. Download skill.zip from the v0.1.0-beta.4 prerelease (all releases: Releases ). Check the SHA-256 in the release notes. The archive contains one folder, inbox-envoy/ , with SKILL.md at its root. Give it to your agent using that agent's own skill or custom-instruction import. Hosts that load skills from a folder on disk usually want the unzipped inbox-envoy/ folder in their skills directory. Exact steps vary by host. See COMPATIBILITY.md for the required host capabilities and safe modes. Install the Inbox Envoy skill from the attached ZIP or this repository using your supported skill workflow. Read SKILL.md . Check your actual mailbox, scheduler, state, and research capabilities, then walk me through onboarding. Start in Observe with no mailbox changes and no external contact. Show the operational readiness report. Do not schedule or change anything until I approve. Expect a read-only start. The agent should explain its modes, show what it can actually do, preview a few classifications, and ask before any label, schedule, research or outbound step. If it claims capabilities it has not verified, stop and ask it to check. Full first-run expectations are in INSTALL.md . Both install the same SKILL.md and references. Installing

story|ver:29.90|title:sub 30s llm pretra.content_excerpt: A third Track 1 modded-nanogpt record attempt, building on @caraxesml's #404: six small, exact GPU fixes (+175 lines) cross below 30 seconds at 29.90 s across 12 runs vs 30.05 s for #404 on the same 8×H100 node. In review as PRs #406 and #407. ⚠️ This is a record attempt , built on other people's work. It is submitted as PR #406 (code) and PR #407 (runs and logs), and both are in review. It only becomes an official record if the maintainers verify it on their own hardware. All numbers below are from one rented 8×H100 node on runpod.io . Modded-nanogpt is a community speedrun: train a GPT-2-scale language model from scratch on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs until it reaches a validation loss of 3.28 or lower, as fast as possible. Since 2024, dozens of contributors have taken that run from 45 minutes all the way down to around 30 seconds. Three weeks ago, my second attempt hit 30.67 seconds ( #396 / #397 ). Since then, @caraxesml made another big jump with PR #404 — 30.25 seconds on GKE (and 30.05 seconds on our RunPod node). This third attempt stacks cleanly on #404 with +175 net lines across 8 files. Same model, same data, same 1,053 training steps, and the exact same math — just less wasted GPU work. On the same 8×H100 node, it shaves off 145 milliseconds and crosses cleanly under 30 seconds at 29.90 seconds . (Quick note on rules: this is Track 1 , the standard from-scratch pretraining ruleset. Separate retrieval-hybrid tracks like #380 reach 5–10 seconds under different rules that allow exact lookups from training data.) Almost everything that makes this model fast comes from Keller Jordan (who started the speedrun), @francesco-prignano ( PR #393 ), and @caraxesml ( PR #404 ). Because different cloud clusters run at slightly different speeds ( #404 ran 30.25 s on GKE vs 30.05 s on our RunPod node), we timed #404 and our code back-to-back on the exact same machine. Modern GPUs are extraordinarily fast at arithmetic, so they often spend their time waiting on memory traffic or tiny setup overheads rather than math. Two simple ideas account for most of our 145 ms gain: To rule out hardware drift, we ran 4 interleaved rounds on one RunPod 8×H100 node ( 1 × #404 , then 3 × this PR ), with random seeds and zero runs dropped: Half of our "clever" ideas failed once we measured them on real hardware.
